content: 1. The WHO guidelines outline various health domains addressed by digital health interventions, including birth notification, death notification, stock notification and commodity management, client-to-provider telemedicine, provider-to-provider telemedicine, targeted client communication via mobile devices, health worker decision support, digital tracking of patients’ health status and services, and the provision of educational and training content to health workers. 2. Birth notifications are recommended in settings where they provide individual-level data to the health system or a civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) system, and where the health system or CRVS system has the capacity to respond to these notifications. This includes initiating postnatal services and triggering birth registration and certification processes. 3. Death notifications are recommended in the context of rigorous research and in settings where they provide individual-level data to the health system or CRVS system, and where these systems can respond appropriately. This includes validating information to trigger death registration and certification processes. 4. Digital stock notification and commodity management are recommended in settings where supply chain management systems can respond in a timely and appropriate manner to stock notifications, ensuring the availability of health commodities and supplies at the point of care. 5. Client-to-provider telemedicine is recommended to complement, rather than replace, traditional health service delivery. It should be implemented in settings where patient safety, privacy, traceability, accountability, and security can be monitored, with protocols in place for patient consent, data protection, and provider credential verification. 6. Provider-to-provider telemedicine is recommended in settings where similar safeguards for patient safety, privacy, and accountability are in place, ensuring secure and effective communication between healthcare providers. 7. Targeted client communication via mobile devices is recommended for addressing health issues related to sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health, provided that concerns about sensitive content and data privacy are adequately addressed. 8. Digital decision support tools accessible via mobile devices are recommended for community and facility-based health workers, specifically for tasks already defined within their scope of practice. 9. Digital tracking of clients’ health status and services, combined with decision support, is recommended in settings where the health system can support integrated implementation of these components and for tasks within the health worker’s defined scope of practice. 10. Digital tracking combined with decision support and targeted client communication is recommended in settings where the health system can support integrated implementation, for tasks within the health worker’s scope of practice, and where data privacy concerns can be addressed. 11. The digital provision of educational and training content to health workers is recommended to complement traditional methods of delivering continued health education and post-certification training. 12. Mobile devices are widely used in lowand middle-income countries, driving research and investment in digital health interventions. Their portability offers unique opportunities for service delivery, particularly in geographically inaccessible areas. 13. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of evidence-based digital health interventions to strengthen health systems and contribute to universal health coverage (UHC). These interventions should be accessible via mobile devices at a minimum but can also be delivered through other digital platforms. 14. The guidelines integrate existing WHO recommendations where relevant and provide additional context and citations for source documents to ensure clarity and applicability. 15. Digital health interventions are expected to contribute to UHC by improving accountability, quality, and accessibility of health services. They aim to ensure that health workers provide high-quality care, individuals can access health services and information, and health commodities are available at the point of care. 16. The WHO underscores the need for rigorous evaluation of digital health technologies to ensure they do not divert resources from alternative, non-digital approaches and to assess their impact on health systems and population well-being.
